name: Treaty with the Kaskaskia, Peoria, etc., 1854
aka: Treaty with the united Kaskaskia, Peoria, Piankeshaw and Wea, May 30, 1854
nations: Peoria Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma (the united Kaskaskia, Peoria, Piankeshaw and Wea)
promises: The United States recognized the Kaskaskia, Peoria, Piankeshaw and Wea as one united tribe (Article 1).
160 acres reserved for each member and ten sections held in common, out of the Kansas lands ceded (Article 2).
The rest of the ceded land offered at public auction under the public land laws, with all the money from the sales, less costs, paid to the tribe (Article 4).
No outsiders allowed to locate or settle on the ceded country until the Indians had made their selections (Article 8).

breaches.what: The Indian Claims Commission found that the United States did not sell the ceded lands on a freely competitive market as Article 4 required, but let settlers claim tracts at appraised values; it found the 207,758.85 acres sold in June and July 1857 would have averaged $2.50 an acre ($519,397.13) against $346,671.09 realized, and awarded the $172,726.04 difference.

landTaken: Royce Areas 326, 327 and 328 in eastern Kansas, granted under the two Castor Hill treaties of October 1832; 207,758.85 acres were sold in June and July 1857 (Docket 65 findings, 1965).
compensation: $346,671.09 from the 1857 sales; Commission award of $171,896.90 net in 1965. The Commission refused interest on the ground that no statute or contract required it.
today: The Commission found that squatters, investors and speculators moved onto the ceded lands after the treaty, helped by the Kansas-Nebraska Act passed the same day and the extension of pre-emption to Kansas on 22 July 1854, though it did not find they interfered with the Indian selections.
